The green sea urchin Psammechinus miliaris begins life as a fertilised egg following broadcast fertilisation in the water column. The resulting zygote develops into a free-swimming pluteus larva that feeds planktotrophically on phytoplankton. After a period of growth in the plankton, the larva reaches metamorphic competence and undergoes larval metamorphosis, during which the bilateral body plan is reorganised into the radial symmetry of the juvenile. For individuals reared at a constant temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the time since birth at this metamorphic transition has been documented at approximately 45 days . The newly metamorphosed juvenile, weighing a mere 0.00048 grams  in wet mass, begins a benthic existence marked by grazing on algal films. The initial wet weight at birth, recorded immediately after the fertilised ovum stage, is an extraordinarily minute 0.0000005 grams [Wwb = 0.0000005 grams], reflecting the minuscule size of the egg cell.

Juvenile Psammechinus miliaris continue to grow through a prolonged sub-adult phase, gradually increasing their test diameter as they forage on coralline algae and small invertebrates. The length at metamorphosis, which corresponds to the test diameter of the recently settled individual, has been estimated at 0.09 centimeters  based on allometric relationships derived from data on the closely related species Echinus esculentus. The growth trajectory accelerates during the first year of benthic life as the juvenile sea urchin accumulates somatic tissue. At a water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the time since birth at puberty is reached after approximately 365 days [tp = approximately 365 days], at which point the individual’s gonads become capable of gametogenesis. At this pubertal stage, the test diameter at puberty measures roughly 0.9 centimeters [Lp = roughly 0.9 centimeters], a size that appears to be a consistent threshold for the onset of reproductive activation across multiple populations studied in the field. The corresponding wet weight at puberty is 0.365 grams [Wwp = 0.365 grams], a value derived from the length-weight scaling relationship established for this species.

Once sexual maturation is completed, Psammechinus miliaris enters its reproductive phase as a spawning adult capable of participating in annual breeding events. The maximum recorded reproductive output for this species is considerable: females have been observed to release approximately 2,500,000 eggs across the entire spawning season [Ri = approximately 2,500,000 eggs across the entire spawning season] when maintained at a constant thermal regime of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. This represents an extraordinarily high fecundity when compared to other co-occurring echinoids of similar body size, such as Paracentrotus lividus, which typically produce fewer than one million oocytes annually. The annual reproductive effort is concentrated into a single spawning period each year [F_R_i = single spawning period each year], a pattern that aligns with the seasonal phytoplankton blooms in the coastal waters of the northeastern Atlantic where this species is most abundant. The temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C] appears to be near the thermal optimum for gametogenic activity, as fecundity declines sharply at both lower and higher temperatures in laboratory trials.

As Psammechinus miliaris continues to grow beyond the pubertal stage, it eventually approaches its maximum dimensions. The ultimate test diameter, representing the largest horizontal measurement across the test that a fully grown adult can attain under natural conditions, reaches 5.75 centimeters [Li = 5.75 centimeters]. Individuals achieving this maximal size are typically reproductively active adults that have completed several successive spawning seasons and have accrued substantial somatic reserves. The corresponding ultimate wet weight of these large specimens is 75.78 grams [Wwi = 75.78 grams], a mass that reflects the substantial calcified skeleton and well-developed gonadal tissue characteristic of post-pubertal adults. These extreme values are rarely attained in populations subject to intense predation pressure from crabs and starfish, but they have been recorded in protected subtidal habitats where food availability is consistently high and mortality rates are low. The growth trajectory toward this maximum size is asymptotic, with most somatic expansion occurring during the first three to four years of life before the growth rate decelerates markedly in later adulthood.

The complete lifespan of Psammechinus miliaris, from the moment of gamete fusion to natural death, has been estimated through mark-recapture studies and laboratory longevity experiments. When maintained at a stable temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the maximum lifespan is approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years], a duration that places this species among the longer-lived echinoids in the family Parechinidae. Old individuals nearing the end of their lives exhibit signs of physiological death, including progressive test erosion, loss of spine mobility, and reduced feeding activity which ultimately leads to irreversible physiological deterioration. The 10-year lifespan (10 years) [am = 10 years] at 10 °C [T = 10 °C] appears to be largely determined by the slow accumulation of somatic damage associated with a low metabolic rate, a life-history strategy typical of cold-water marine invertebrates. In comparison, the congeneric species Psammechinus microtuberculatus, which inhabits warmer Mediterranean waters, has a reported lifespan of only six to seven years, suggesting that temperature plays a role in modulating longevity across the genus.
